stops.name: USS Constellation
stops.description: The last sail-only warship the U.S. Navy ever built sits at Constellation Dock in the Inner Harbor, open to visitors as part of Historic Ships in Baltimore.

stops.name: National Aquarium
stops.description: The glass-pyramid aquarium on Pier 3 anchored the Inner Harbor's turnaround and is still the harbor's busiest front door.

stops.name: Baltimore World Trade Center
stops.description: The world's tallest pentagonal building, turned so one corner points at the water like a ship's prow, with a public observation deck 27 floors up.

stops.name: Pratt Street Power Plant
stops.description: One of only eleven buildings inside the burn zone to survive the 1904 Baltimore Fire, this coal plant now holds restaurants and offices behind its four smokestacks.

stops.name: Reginald F. Lewis Museum of Maryland African American History & Culture
stops.description: A Smithsonian affiliate whose five-story facade is built in the red, black and gold of the Maryland flag, holding 400 years of Black Maryland history.

stops.name: Flag House & Star-Spangled Banner Museum
stops.description: Mary Young Pickersgill sewed the oversized garrison flag that flew over Fort McHenry in this 1793 house, and the museum next door carries a window-sized replica of it.

stops.name: Carroll Mansion
stops.description: Charles Carroll of Carrollton, the last surviving signer of the Declaration of Independence, spent his final twelve winters here and died in the house.

stops.name: Lloyd Street Synagogue
stops.description: Maryland's first synagogue and the fifth oldest surviving one in the country, with what may be the nation's oldest known mikveh found beneath its floor in 2011.

stops.name: Phoenix Shot Tower
stops.description: Molten lead was dropped 234 feet down this 1828 brick tower to form musket shot, and it was the tallest structure in the United States for eighteen years.

stops.name: President Street Station
stops.description: The oldest surviving big-city railroad terminal in the country, where Lincoln passed through in secret in 1861 and the first blood of the Civil War was spilled weeks later.

stops.name: Baltimore City Hall
stops.description: A 22-year-old architect named George A. Frederick won the commission for this marble Second Empire pile, whose cast-iron dome was taken apart and rebuilt in the 1970s.

stops.name: War Memorial Plaza
stops.description: The open square between City Hall and the War Memorial Building, dedicated to Marylanders lost in World War I and home to James E. Lewis's 1971 Negro Soldier statue.

stops.name: Battle Monument
stops.description: The first public war memorial in the United States lists the Battle of Baltimore's dead regardless of rank, with eighteen marble courses for the eighteen states of 1815.

stops.name: United States Custom House
stops.description: Its Call Room ceiling carries Francis Davis Millet's mural of a ten-ship fleet under sail, part of a scheme showing more than 125 vessels from Egyptian craft to ocean liners.

note: Baltimore, MD - first run for this city; only Atlanta had run before, so this was the alphabetically first untouched NFL host city. The cluster is a tight downtown loop: Inner Harbor north shore, east along Pratt St into Jonestown, then back west to the municipal center at City Hall and Battle Monument. Roughly 0.8 mi across, walkable end to end. Four stops have address null on purpose - Wikipedia gives USS Constellation only as Constellation Dock, Phoenix Shot Tower as Front & Fayette Sts, President Street Station as the junction of President and Fleet Sts, and War Memorial Plaza only by its four bounding streets. No street number was invented for any of them; a human can fill those in. ZIP appears only where an article actually printed it. Dropped as outside the loop: Lexington Market and the Emerson Bromo-Seltzer Tower (both about a half mile further west), and Federal Hill Park plus the American Visionary Art Museum (across the water on Key Highway). Dropped Maryland Science Center - real and open, but its article gives coordinates and no street address. Excluded the Statue of Christopher Columbus (removed from its site in 2020), the Baltimore Public Works Museum and Sports Legends Museum (both closed), and the many list, district, neighborhood and transit-station pages the GeoSearch sweep returned. Baltimore has more than 300 NRHP listings across five sub-lists, so plenty is left for future runs - Mount Vernon Place, the Washington Monument, the Basilica of the Assumption and the Cathedral Hill district would make a good second Baltimore loop.
